name: Frostmere

npcs._note: THE RIVAL SYSTEM PUTS HIM HERE AND THIS MAP ONLY HAS TO GIVE HIM SOMEWHERE TO STAND. The id, the script and the hide-flag are the shared contract in src/systems/tarin.ts and data/events/common.json -- tarin_town branches on tarin_at_frostmere, fights the hardest rival battle in the story and then sets tarin_frostmere_done, which is what takes him off this street. Nothing about him is written here. He is in the middle row of Street One eight tiles inside the gate, because the ledger says he took the Crest on Tuesday and did not leave, and a boy who has been waiting four days is not standing somewhere you have to go and look for him.

text: The gate board, and it is a tally rather than a welcome. Two columns, chalked:
IN TODAY. OUT TODAY. The numbers have to match by dark or somebody goes looking.
Under them, in older paint: WE HAVE NOT LOST ANYBODY SINCE 1849. HELP US KEEP IT.
A card wired to the lantern post at the height of somebody holding the rope:
BLUE IS A DOOR. YELLOW IS A WINDOW. IN A WHITEOUT A WINDOW IS A WALL.
WALK AT THE BLUE ONE. IF YOU CANNOT SEE ONE, DO NOT LET GO OF THE CORD.
The inn board, and it is not a menu. One line, painted very large:
IF YOUR FIRE IS OUT, COME HERE. WE WILL NOT ASK AND WE WILL NOT SAY.
The paint has been gone over so many times the letters stand off the wood.
Cut into the lintel of the Hall, deeper than anything else in this town:
THE WATER UNDER THIS HOUSE IS THE TOWN’S. THE HOUSE IS ONLY OVER IT.
Somebody keeps the letters clear of ice. You can see where the chisel goes.
The ice house. No window in it anywhere, and the walls are two feet of sawdust.
A tally by the door: BLOCKS IN. BLOCKS OUT. SOLD TO, and then eleven town names.
This year’s IN column has been started, crossed out and started again four times.
A depth board standing in the stacks, marked off in inches from the bottom.
CUTTING THICKNESS: TWELVE. Every winter since 1802 is scratched down the side.
The last three read fourteen, then eleven, then a mark at five with no year on it.
A trail board where the wood closes over the track, weathered nearly smooth:
THE OBSERVATORY. FOUR HOURS UP. NO WATER, NO SHELTER, NO SECOND ROUTE.
Under it, in a much newer hand: AND NOBODY UP THERE TO MEET YOU. GO ANYWAY.
The first cairn above the treeline, and the stones on it are not all one age.
A slate wired to the top: FOR THE ONES THE MOUNTAIN KEPT. Nine names under it.
The rest of the slate is blank and ruled, which is somehow the worst part of it.
A wire fence, a mast and a generator running, on a shoulder where nothing else is.
A plate on the gate: MERIDIAN FOUNDATION — UPPER CAELORA WEATHER STATION.
Every instrument on it is pointed at the sky. The cable from them runs uphill.
The doorway is cut square into the rock and there is nothing hung in it.
No hinge, no jamb, no seating for a bar. Whoever built this did not fit a door,
and the stone is dressed too well everywhere else for that to be an oversight.

_plan:
A TOWN BUILT BY PEOPLE WHO EXPECT THE WEATHER TO TRY TO KILL THEM. Everything
on this map is downstream of that one sentence.

THREE OF ITS COORDINATES ARE NOT MINE AND THE PLAN IS BUILT ROUND THEM.
route_8_pass puts the player down at 2,24 / 2,25 / 2,26, so STREET ONE is three
rows deep -- which is also the honest reason for it, since this is the only line
Frostmere sweeps all winter and it is cut wide enough for two loaded ice sledges
to pass. frostmere_observatory comes back out at 20,6, so the Aurelian doorway
is cut into the rock at 20,5 with their apron running down to the trail at 20,8.
Both of those files were already on disk when this one was laid out.

THE WALLS ARE A METRE THICK AND THE HOUSES SHARE THEM. Frostmere is not a street
of cottages, it is terraces: one long building either side of the road, because
a shared wall is a wall nobody is heating, and at three thousand people in a
valley this cold that is arithmetic rather than taste. The stone is the mountain
the town is hiding from, and it is the darkest built material in the game
standing in the brightest ground in the game. That is the silhouette of the
place, and it is why the Frostmere tiles are a BUILDING set that adds nothing to
the snow the mountain roads already own.

EVERY DOOR IS RECESSED AND EVERY DOOR FACES SOUTH. A door flush with a wall opens
against a drift and does not open at all, and the wind comes off the pass. So the
doors are cut back into the thickness of their own wall with a hood over them,
and every one is in the south face of its terrace. That is why there are two
streets: the north terrace opens onto Street One and the shore terrace opens onto
the quay road, because they could not both face the one.

THE LANTERNS ARE BLUE BECAUSE A YELLOW ONE KILLS PEOPLE. A warm lamp and a lit
window are the same colour through falling snow, and somebody who walks at a
window in a whiteout dies against a wall. The rule is BLUE MEANS DOOR. The tile
carries its rope out of both sides of its cell, so the lanterns on this map are
always laid in RUNS ALONG A ROAD, a rope length apart, and never scattered as
decoration: in a bad week you do not walk between the lights, you hold the cord
that joins them.

THE MERE IS THE ECONOMY AND THE MERE IS THE STORM. Frostmere sells winter -- sawn
lake ice packed in straw, south, to eleven towns with no other way to keep
anything cold. The ice house has no window in it anywhere. And the outer half of
the lake is ROTTEN ICE, which is solid, so a player who walks out onto the mere
gets four tiles and then a wall of white stars over black water. That is Act 5
stated in terrain before one word of dialogue: the lake did not freeze this year,
the crews are standing about, and the depth board on the quay says the same thing
in numbers.

THE FOUNDATION IS ALREADY UP THERE. A wire compound, a mast and a generator
running on the shelf above the town, with a Foundation coat inside it. Nothing in
Frostmere dialogue joins that to the weather. The map puts the two facts on one
screen and lets the player draw the line.

THE TREELINE AT ROW 13 IS LOAD-BEARING. Above it there is no way up except the
trail, so the shelf under the rock is not somewhere a player wanders into off the
back of the town -- it is somewhere they went. That is the whole reason a
four-hour climb reads as a climb on a map forty-six rows tall.
